name: Tamil Nadu
description: The cradle of Dravidian temple handlooms, revered for heavy mulberry Kanchipuram silks, pure zari borders, and Chettinad weaves.
heritageStory: For over four centuries, master weavers believed to be descendants of Sage Markanda—the weaver of the Gods—have spun gold and silk in the temple town of Kanchipuram. Incorporating ancient Dravidian architectural motifs like the Gopuram (temple tower), peacock, and Mayilkan, these sarees are woven with the legendary Korvai interlocking technique.

name: Uttar Pradesh
description: Home to the eternal sacred looms of Varanasi and the delicate Nawabi embroidery courtyards of Lucknow.
heritageStory: Banarasi brocade weaving flourished under the royal patronage of the Mughal dynasty when Persian artisans merged their intricate floral arabesques with ancient Indian silk traditions. Concurrently, the royal begums of Awadh nurtured Chikankari—a poetry of needlework featuring thirty-six distinct hand stitches.

name: Telangana
description: A land of geometric genius with Pochampally double ikat and the royal grandeur of Gadwal silk-cotton hybrid weaves.
heritageStory: In Bhoodan Pochampally, weavers perform an extraordinary feat of mental geometry—dyeing warp and weft threads before weaving so that when interlaced on the loom, complex diamond matrices align with razor-sharp accuracy. In Gadwal, the unique Kuttu technique joins a lightweight cotton body with sumptuous silk borders.

name: Andhra Pradesh
description: Famed for the gossamer Jamdani of Uppada, royal Dharmavaram silks, and crisp Mangalagiri cottons.
heritageStory: Along the coastal delta of East Godavari, Uppada Jamdani weavers craft sarees so light they float like morning mist, weaving intricate non-structural weft motifs without any mechanical punch cards. Meanwhile, Dharmavaram weavers near the Anantapur plateau produce lavish bridal silks famed for their broad contrast pallus.

name: Karnataka
description: The Silk Capital of India, home to Mysore crepe silks, royal gold zari, and rustic Ilkal weaves.
heritageStory: Established in 1912 by Maharaja Nalvadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar of Mysore with looms imported from Switzerland, Mysore Silk represents the pinnacle of luxurious crepe drape. The pure gold electroplated borders and lightweight 100% natural silk remain the hallmark of South Indian nobility.

name: Maharashtra
description: Regal Paithani drapes of the Maratha empire, known as the 'Golden Queen' of Indian heirlooms.
heritageStory: Originating over 2,000 years ago in Pratishthana on the banks of Godavari, Paithani sarees were cherished by Satavahana rulers and the Peshwas. Handcrafted using a tapestry weave where multiple color wefts interlock manually, its signature Asavali (flowering vine) and Morbangadi (peacock in bangle) borders take months of patient devotion.

name: Gujarat
description: Celebrated for Patan Patola double ikat, vivid Bandhani tie-dye, and traditional Gharchola wedding drapes.
heritageStory: Patan Patola is one of the world's most intricate textile arts, created by the Salvi community where both warp and weft are tie-dyed in natural vegetable pigments before touching the loom. A famous Gujarati proverb says: 'Padi patole bhat, fatey pan phitey nahin'—the design may tear with time, but the color shall never fade.

name: Rajasthan
description: A celebration of desert royalty featuring airy Kota Doria, Leheriya ripple dyes, and glistening Gota Patti embellishments.
heritageStory: Against the golden sands of the Thar desert, Rajasthan weaves vivid rainbows. Kota Doria originated when Rao Kishore Singh brought weavers from Mysore to Kota in the 17th century. The signature Khat weave creates light squares that keep the wearer cool under the royal desert sun.

name: West Bengal
description: The poetic weaves of Bengal: aristocratic Baluchari narrating epics, fine muslin Jamdani, and organic Linen.
heritageStory: Bengal weaving is rich with literary and mythological expression. Baluchari pallus depict scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Nawabi courts woven in untwisted silk floss. Concurrently, Dhaka-Bengal Jamdani is recognized by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

name: Odisha
description: Sacred Baandha ikat weaves intimately tied to Lord Jagannath culture, Bomkai, and Sambalpuri handlooms.
heritageStory: Every thread of an Odia saree is touched by bhakti and nature. Weavers from Sambalpur and Bargarh tie-dye threads with calligraphic precision, depicting Shankha (conch), Chakra (disc), fish, lotus, and the temple chariot. In Khandua silk sarees, verses from Jayadeva's Gita Govinda are woven directly into the fabric.

name: Madhya Pradesh
description: The translucent splendor of Chanderi and the regal architectural borders of Maheshwari sarees.
heritageStory: Founded according to legend by Lord Krishna's cousin Shishupal, Chanderi weaving was patronized by the Scindias of Gwalior. Its sheer tissue texture is achieved using degummed raw silk and fine count cotton. Along the Narmada river, Queen Ahilyabai Holkar designed Maheshwari sarees inspired by the river fort ramparts.

name: Kerala
description: God's Own Country's iconic Kasavu handloom: unbleached organic kora cotton adorned with pure gold zari.
heritageStory: Kasavu sarees are the essence of Onam, Vishu, and temple rituals in Kerala. Woven in Balaramapuram and Kuthampully, the pristine natural cream cotton body contrasts against shimmering pure gold zari borders, epitomizing sovereign simplicity and coastal grace.

name: Assam
description: The golden glory of Muga silk—the naturally shimmering silk found nowhere else on earth—and Eri Ahimsa silk.
heritageStory: Known as the pride of the Brahmaputra valley, Muga silk is produced by silkworms endemic to Assam that feed on som and soalu leaves. The resulting fiber possesses a luminous golden amber hue that actually grows more lustrous with every wash, woven into traditional Kingkhap and floral motifs.

name: Bihar
description: World-famous Bhagalpuri Tussar wild silk and exquisite hand-painted Madhubani Mithila art sarees.
heritageStory: Bhagalpur has been known as the 'Silk City' for over a century, producing natural textured Tussar silk. In the Mithila region, women artisans use bamboo nibs and natural vegetable pigments to hand-paint sacred Madhubani narratives of Ram-Sita, tree of life, and celestial motifs directly onto the woven silk.

name: Other Indian States
description: Celebrating regional masterworks from Kashmir's Aari needlework to Goa's Kunbi cottons and Punjab's Phulkari.
heritageStory: India's saree tapestry spans every valley and coast. From the royal court drapes of Jammu & Kashmir featuring delicate Pashmina wool silk and fine Sozni or Aari needlecraft, to Goa's tribal red-and-white Kunbi drapes worn by indigenous Kunbi women, every corner of India tells its story through the loom.
